segments.title: A fictional nuclear coercion plan without a working remote detonator
segments.summary: A shelf-building aside recalls an unnamed geopolitical thriller in which a covert Russian nuclear operation against Japan fails because the weapons have no viable remote-detonation system.
segments.body: An aside during the shelf build turns to an unnamed geopolitical thriller rather than a real Russia-Japan war. In the story, a deniable Russian mission uses a diesel submarine and commandos to place nuclear weapons in a Japanese harbor, recalled here as Tokyo Bay. The weapons are meant to coerce Japan through the threat of remote detonation. A poorly made box reveals that the operation has no working remote control or detonator. Once that flaw is exposed, the weapons can be disarmed. The story illustrates a practical strategic problem: secrecy and access cannot rescue a coercive plan when its equipment and command link do not work.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke describes an unnamed book's fictional war between Russia and Japan, a deniable Russian operation, a diesel submarine, commandos, and nuclear weapons.
He explains that a poorly made box exposed the absence of a working remote detonator, allowing the submarine crew to disarm the weapons.
He closes by connecting the plot's technical failure to a joke about the quality of a villain's carpenters.
